description: Every year, the Earth experiences hundreds of thousands of earthquakes. Most are invisible. A few change entire cities.

hero.hook: An earthquake is not a whim of the ground. This is an energy that has waited too long.

blocks.text: Each year, the Earth records approximately **500,000 detectable earthquakes**. Only a small part causes big damage. An earthquake is not a coincidence: it is the sudden end of a long accumulation of energy in the rocks.
To understand this, we must see the surface of the planet as a puzzle of moving plates. Where these plates rub together, tension builds…until it breaks.

The earth's surface is divided into around ten large **tectonic plates**. They slide on a softer layer of the coat, the . Their speed? About **1 to 10 cm per year**, about the same as the growth of a fingernail. [[Asthenosphere]]

blocks.caption: Earthquakes suddenly release the energy accumulated along faults.

blocks.text: At the borders, three scenarios dominate. The plates are moving apart (oceanic ridges). They collide: sometimes one dives under the other, it's . Or they slide side by side, like along the [[Subduction]] in California, approximately **1 300 km** long. [[The San Andreas Fault]]
Along the San Andreas, Los Angeles gets closer to San Francisco by about **6 cm** per year. In **15 million years**, the two cities would be neighbors.
It is especially at these borders that earthquakes occur. The movement of the plates is hindered by the friction of the rocks. Energy accumulates silently.
An earthquake occurs along a **fault**: a fracture between two blocks of rock. In theory, the plates should slide continuously. In practice, friction often blocks this sliding.
During this time, the plaques continue to grow. The rock deforms a little, like a bow being drawn. We speak of elastic constraints. This can last decades, sometimes centuries.

When the resistance limit is exceeded, the blocks suddenly slide. The energy leaves in the form of **eismic waves**. The depth break point is called the **focus**. On the surface, the point just above is the **epicenter**, where the effects are often strongest.

To measure the energy of an earthquake, seismologists mainly use the moment . It's a logarithmic scale: each degree multiplies the energy by approximately **32**. An earthquake of magnitude **8** therefore releases approximately **1,000 times** more energy than an earthquake of magnitude **6**. [[The magnitude scale (Richter/Moment)]]
There are also earthquakes of **0** or negative magnitude. These are very small events, visible only with very sensitive sensors.

The strongest ever measured with modern instruments is that of **Valdivia**, in Chile, in **1960**: magnitude **9.5**. If the focus is under the ocean and raises the seafloor, the displaced water column can create a **tsunami**. In **2004**, an earthquake of magnitude **9.1** near Sumatra triggered a tsunami that struck 14 countries and claimed approximately **227,000** lives.

After the breakup, several types of waves leave. The **P waves** (primary) arrive first: they compress the rock like an accordion. Then come the **ZZ** (secondary) waves, slower and often more destructive. The surface waves then cause the ground to oscillate very visibly.

We do not yet know how to predict the exact day of a major earthquake. On the other hand, we map the risk areas.  designs buildings capable of withstanding shocks: mobile foundations, giant shock absorbers, structures that absorb energy. In Japan, early warnings detect P waves and can cut off gas or slow trains before the most dangerous waves arrive. [[Seismic engineering]]
An earthquake occurs when rocks stuck along a fault suddenly release decades of tension. Energy travels in waves, and each degree of magnitude multiplies that energy by approximately **32**.
